blocks.content:
3 very ripe bananas
    1/4 cup smooth natural peanut butter
    1 teaspoon vanilla extract
    1 1/4 cup instant or quick cooking oats
    1/4 teaspoon salt
    1/2 teaspoon baking powder
    1/2 cup chocolate chips

Instructions 

    Preheat the oven to 350 F. Grease a loaf pan or line with parchment paper.
    Add the bananas to a large bowl and mash until almost smooth. Add in the peanut butter and vanilla extract and mix well.
    Add in the oats, salt, and baking powder and mix to combine. Fold in 1/3 cup of the chocolate chips, reserving the rest for the top of the bars.
    Pour the mixture into the loaf pan, using a spoon or spatula to smooth it out on top. Add the remaining chocolate chips to the top of the bars. Bake for 25-30 minutes, until a knife inserted in the center comes out clean.
    Let cool and cut into 6-8 pieces.

Ingredients

    280 grams all-purpose flour 2 cups
    240 grams active or sourdough discard 1 cup
    120 grams milk 1/2 cup
    4 grams baking powder 1 teaspoon
    6 grams salt 1 teaspoon
    15 grams olive oil 1 Tablespoon
    olive oil for frying

Instructions

Create the Dough
  + To a large bowl, add the flour, sourdough starter (active or discard), milk, baking powder, salt and olive oil.
  + 280 grams all-purpose flour, 240 grams active or sourdough discard, 120 grams milk, 4 grams baking powder, 6 grams salt, 15 grams olive oil
   + Mix until most of the flour has been incorporated.
   + I like to mix the ingredients with a Danish dough whisk, but you can also do so with a wooden spoon or by hand.
   + Remove the dough from the bowl and place it on a lightly floured work surface.

Knead the Dough
   + To knead the dough, pull a piece up and then fold it towards the center and press the heel of your hand into the dough.
   + Turn the dough clockwise a quarter turn. Repeat for about 2-3 minutes. The dough may look a little lumpy, but that is okay.
   + If the dough is looking dry, sprinkle a little extra water. If the dough is sticky, sprinkle a little extra flour.

Leave to rest
   + If you are using an active sourdough starter, place the dough in a greased bowl and cover it with plastic wrap, or I like to use a reusable shower cap.
   + Leave in a warm place to long ferment and at least double in size. In my 70 degree F kitchen I leave it for 18-24 hours. If you kitchen is cooler, it will take longer to ferment. If your kitchen is warmer, it will ferment faster.
   + If you are using sourdough discard, cover the dough with a clean tea towel and let the dough rest for at least 30 minutes. I've left it for longer – 2-4 hours. This allows the gluten to relax so it is easier to stretch.

Shape and Fry
   + Once the dough has rested, take a bench scraper or sharp knife and cut it into 8 equal parts. I will cut the dough into quarters and then cut each piece in half. They don't have to be perfectly equal pieces, just eyeball them.
   + Before you begin rolling out the dough balls, sprinkle a little extra flour on your work surface and on the rolling pin.
   + Roll out each dough ball one at a time. You want them pretty thin, about a 1/8 inch. They don't have to be a perfect circle to be perfectly tasty!
   + Preheat your cast iron pan to medium heat. Grease the hot pan with a little bit of olive oil or vegetable oil.
   + Place one flatbread in the cast iron at a time. Cook for a couple of minutes. The dough will start to bubble and puff up.
   + Before I flip to the other side, I like to pour a little olive oil on top of the flatbread for extra flavor and blisters. Flip and cook for 1-2 minutes more.
   + Remove from the pan and repeat until all of the sourdough flatbread has been cooked. Enjoy!

Recipe Tips
   + Sourdough flatbread will stay fresh for up to 2 days at room temperature. Store in an airtight container or sealed bag for optimal freshness. After the second day, you can store them in the refrigerator till day 5. Reheat in a frying pan on low heat until pliable and warm.
   + If the stovetop is occupied, the oven will do the trick! Preheat your oven to 500 degrees F and lay your flatbread on a baking sheet. Cook the flatbread for 3-4 minutes on each side or until puffed and brown. Since you are not using oil as you would in the skillet, the flatbread may be a bit crispier.
   + For some added flavors, sprinkle in some shredded cheese, minced garlic or onion, dried herbs, or even some everything bagel seasoning just before you are about to knead the dough. For a sweet version, sprinkle them with cinnamon and sugar once you pull them from the frying pan.

Hey. I'm here. What's on your mind today?

I don't what it is about watching tv with mom, but it always gets me feeling...overwhelmed? idk. I know part of it is just the tv being louder than what I like, and she talks a lot. And if it's even the slightest bit cold, the heater is on that dries my already dry skin, so then I'm itchy and hot. 
Anywho, just trying this out in the app I'm building. Trying to make my ultimate planner/journal/tracker/therapy. It's going pretty well so far.

So you know exactly what's making you overwhelmed — the volume, the talking, the heat, the itchiness. Those are all real sensory things piling up on you. But you're still sitting there doing it. 

Why? Is it because you want to spend time with her, or because you feel like you should? And have you actually told her any of this — that the TV's too loud, that you're uncomfortable — or are you just enduring it?

Also, cool that you're building this. What made you want to create it yourself instead of using something that already exists?

Because I know she likes it. She's an extrovert who needs to socialize. But she has lots of health issues, so it's hard for her to go do things. She only drives locally. So I know she appreciates any time spent together. However I'm an introvert, so any time spent together drains me. 
She's ok with the volume going down (we have captions on, which I do like), but temperature is something that has never been negotiable. Before it was just preference, but now it's also health related. 
I don't to pay for an app that doesn't do what I want, and pretty much everything requires a subscription these days. I wanted a planner, but also a journal, and anything else I think of. You're really good at coding and making this super easy.

You're being thoughtful about her needs, which is good. But let's be honest — you're treating this like there are only two options: endure the sensory overload to make her happy, or don't spend time with her at all.

Have you actually suggested doing something *different* together? Something that doesn't trap you in a hot room with loud TV? Even if her mobility is limited, there are other ways to be together. A quieter activity. Sitting outside if weather permits. A short drive together where *you* control the environment. 

You're framing this as sacrifice, but it sounds more like you haven't really problem-solved it. You've just accepted the setup that makes you miserable.

And here's the thing — if spending time with her always leaves you drained and uncomfortable, you're eventually going to start avoiding it. Then nobody wins.

What would actually work better for both of you?

I think this is the best. We do not agree on politics, and she is big on tying politics into everything. So being stuck in the car with her nonstop talking is worse, for sure. Watching tv keeps things light and focused on what we're watching. 
I mean, sometimes we go shopping, but I'm not big on that either. Stores are kinda gross, and in the winter they're hot and dry as well. 
She will talk forever, and it's pretty one-sided. Like, she doesn't really expect or need me to reply. She just wants someone in the room to listen to her. Like, she'll ask a question and I'll answer it, only for her to either talk over me, or tell me I'm wrong.

Okay, so this paints a clearer picture. It's not just about the TV or the temperature — it's that spending time with her in *any* form is draining because of how she interacts. She dominates the conversation, dismisses what you say, and makes it one-sided. The TV setup is actually the *least bad* option because it gives you both something external to focus on instead of her monologuing at you.

That's fair. But let's call it what it is: you're not really spending quality time together. You're providing her with a warm body in the room so she doesn't feel alone. Which is kind of you, but it's also... not sustainable if it's making you this uncomfortable.

So here's the question: How often are you doing this? And is there a limit where you'd say "I can handle this once a week but not every night," or are you just white-knuckling through whenever she wants company?

Also — have you ever actually told her, plainly, "I feel talked over when I try to answer your questions"? Or are you conflict-avoidant enough that you've never named it?

I think it's just been worse the last few weeks because of the Winter Olympics. We've been watching tv together every night, compared to once or twice a week. With the added bonus of her missing something and me having to fill her in (what country are they from? What score did they get?). So normally it's not this much and not so demanding.
I have talked to her about the talking over, and she did acknowledge that she usually isn't expecting an answer, she's just thinking out loud. 
But I am pretty conflict avoidant overall.

Okay, that makes more sense. The Olympics are a temporary surge, not the baseline. Once they're over, you'll go back to once or twice a week, which you can probably handle without losing your mind.

But here's what I'm hearing: you know this is draining, you know it's temporary, and you're choosing to do it because it matters to her. That's actually pretty solid reasoning — as long as you're making that choice consciously and not just out of guilt or obligation.

The conflict-avoidant thing though — that's worth paying attention to. You talked to her about the talking over, which is good. But are you generally able to set boundaries with her when you need to? Like, if the Olympics weren't ending soon and this *was* becoming every night forever, would you be able to say "I need to cut back to twice a week"?

Or would you just keep sitting there, itchy and hot and overwhelmed, telling yourself it's fine because she needs it?

I mean, tonight I just said, "I need to take a shower tonight and do the dishes, so I think I'm done" and it was no issue. But it was the closing ceremony and it was pretty dull after a while (we did talk about the costumes, and especially Johnny Weir and Tara getting all dressed up every night, and even coordinating their outfits).

Okay, so you *can* set a boundary when you need to, and she respects it. That's actually really important. You're not trapped — you just don't always exercise the option to leave.

So here's what I'm seeing: This situation isn't actually as bad as it felt when you started writing. The Olympics made it feel like too much because it was every night, but you were able to say "I'm done" tonight without drama. Normally it's manageable. And the TV setup, while not ideal, is the best version of spending time with her given the alternatives.

The real question is: Are you giving yourself permission to tap out *before* you hit overwhelm? Or are you waiting until you're itchy, hot, and mentally exhausted before you let yourself leave?

Because it sounds like she'd be fine with you saying "I'm good for an hour tonight" instead of waiting until you're at your limit.

2026-03-02.content: There's so much horrible happening and morning to be done about it. Like, the systems are so big, the corporations are so big, and people are so small. I can only control/change/affect what's immediately around me.
Something went wrong. Please try again.

There's so much horrible happening and morning to be done about it. Like, the systems are so big, the corporations are so big, and people are so small. I can only control/change/affect what's immediately around me.

That feeling of smallness against these massive systems... it sounds really heavy to carry.

When you say you can only affect what's immediately around you — does that feel like a limitation you're frustrated by, or more like something you're trying to accept?

Hmm, I guess acceptance? That I'm not a main character is some young adult dystopian future novel who is destined to save the world from the the evil overlord and bring about utopia? I cannot effect change on a large scale, but I can change what's around me. I can make my home a safe haven for the outcast I come across, I can give to those around me, I try to shape my community to reflect what I believe is right (live justly, be kind, walk humbly, love others as you love yourself, don't judge). 
I can hope that there are others like me. I can hope that together we slowly change the course of the world. 
I was reading Darth Plagueis today and it was describing a big party that was secretly hosted by a Sith lord. It was a party for elites only, where they come together and plan how to influence politics, etc to gain more power and wealth for themselves. It was revolting, and almost laughable because as they showed one character ask about where the host sourced his dancers I thought "geez, we've learned this same thing is happening for real, but it's worse than this!" It's awful what mankind has become. But if you reflect on history, has there ever been a time of just peace? I'm sure there's been little pockets, but there's always some power-hungry fuck who has to ruin everything. What must have happened to them to bring them to that point? 
I guess we at least have modern medicine. But if you live in the wrong place, you have to choose between crippling debt or getting medical care. If you live in another wrong place, you don't even have that medical care. 
The story of the tower of babel comes to mind: are we better off as small tribes, where our whole world is just like 100 people? It seems that as soon as we organize and come together, greed runs in to take over.

You're tracing something really interesting here — this thread from acceptance of your own scale, to wondering about those "others like me," to these big historical patterns, and then that question at the end about whether humans are even meant to organize at this size.

That Tower of Babel thought... are you wondering if there's something about scale itself that breaks us? Like maybe we're wired for those 100-person worlds, and beyond that, the greed you're noticing just becomes inevitable?

And I'm curious about that line — "what must have happened to them to bring them to that point?" When you think about the power-hungry people, does wondering about their story change how it all feels, or does it just add another layer of sad to it?

I think at a smaller scale, there's more social pressure to conform, to behave, so you're not cast out on your own, maybe? Narcissists and power hungry and greedy people still exist at that scale, but everything is more personal. You can't burn bridges so easily. Or you burn the bridge as you're on your way to the next town over. 

I'm thinking that people aren't born seeking power or wealth. That it's a reaction to something that happened. I mean, I guess actual psychopaths are born like that. But is narcissism a from birth thing? I mean, little babies can be greedy, toddlers are definitely jealous and will fight to take what they desire. But on a whole, humans agree that is bad behavior. Someone with no extreme mental health issues would see a toddler act like that and correct their behavior. Or, if you saw an adult encourage that in a toddler, you would think "what's wrong with that person??" 
But it does add another layer of sad because you know they experienced enough pain in their life that they're now twisted and perverted. They don't care who gets hurt as long as they gain something.

There's something in what you're saying about scale and visibility — that at 100 people, you can't hide behind systems or distance. The consequences of your greed are right there in front of you, in the faces of people you'll see tomorrow.

And then this other thread about how people get twisted... like somewhere between "toddler grabbing a toy" and "billionaire hoarding wealth while people suffer," something goes terribly wrong in how pain gets processed. 

You said "they experienced enough pain that they're now twisted and perverted" — does knowing that make you feel anything different toward them? Or is it more like... you can hold both things at once: understanding how they got there AND being revolted by what they do with it?

I'm also sitting with your question about whether we're just not built for this scale. Like maybe the same traits that help a small group survive — ambition, competition, resource-gathering — become monstrous when they're operating across millions of people and billions of dollars.

I can hold both at once. I do struggle with this: at what point is their behavior no longer excusable because of the abuse they were dealt? At some point to you have to stop thinking "I'm the victim, I'm not to blame for my behavior" and work on fixing the damage done to yourself. I think it's easier to fix the younger you are. The less time you live in that brokenness. But that's hard to do when you're young, especially if you're still in that environment that's hurting you. 
I think at a certain point, the scale is large enough that you can disappear into the crowd and become anonymous. You lose that face-face accountability. You lose a sense of community, of needing other people to survive. When there's enough people to carry the burden that you end up with an excess of people with who don't need to contribute, who don't need to think of the whole group, but just themselves.

You're wrestling with something really hard here — that line between "this happened to you" and "but you're still responsible for what you do with it." And the unfairness of it all: that the people most damaged are often the ones still trapped in the situation that's damaging them, with the least resources to heal.

That phrase you used — "living in that brokenness" — there's something about time in it, isn't there? Like the longer someone operates from that broken place, the more it becomes who they are, not just what happened to them.

And then you're connecting it back to scale again. When you're anonymous in the crowd, when you don't *need* your community to survive... does something fundamental break? Like we lose the natural check on behavior that comes from interdependence?

It makes me wonder what you're sitting with underneath all this. Is it the frustration of watching people with power act from their brokenness and hurt everyone else? Or something about trying to figure out where compassion ends and accountability begins?

It's seeing people in power break an already imperfect system just to gain more wealth that will just sit in their vaults, gain more power that they'll just use to gain more wealth. And wondering if it can be fixed. I mean, I guess there are countries that are doing better than the US. Lots of places in Europe actually provide for their citizens. I'm sure they have issues too, but at least the people who there can go to a doctor because everyone pays taxes to fund healthcare everyone. Geez, is this not a mankind problem but an American problem?? 
Like, I live in Texas. A 2 hour drive is nothing. I drive an hour round trip to go to the grocery store. But in Europe, they aren't car dependent. Things are within walking distance. They're not living as a large a scale as Americans?? If you look at Finland, what's the population of the largest city? Or Denmark? The Netherlands?

Oh, you just shifted something. You went from "this is how humans are at scale" to "wait... maybe this is specifically how *we've* built things here."

Because you're right — there are places where people figured out how to organize large numbers of people without losing that sense of collective responsibility. Where the systems are set up assuming interdependence instead of... whatever we're doing.

That car thing is such a concrete example. When your grocery store is an hour round trip, you're dependent on infrastructure but not on *people*. Versus walking to a market where you see your neighbors.

So now I'm curious what this opens up for you. If it's not inevitable that scale breeds that kind of greed and disconnection — if it's more about *how* we've chosen to structure things — does that change how the whole problem feels? Does it make it more fixable, or somehow more frustrating that we're doing it wrong when other places figured it out?
Both! A lot of places have figured it out, so it's not unsolvable. But we're so entrenched, it feels like maybe we'll never be able to change enough to have what other's have.

That's such a particular kind of heaviness — knowing it's *possible* because others did it, but feeling like we're too far down our own path to turn around.

When you say "entrenched," what does that look like in your mind? Is it the physical infrastructure — like all those roads and sprawling suburbs? Or the systems and money behind them? Or something about the culture itself, the way we think about individualism and self-reliance?

Because there's something almost tragic in "we built it wrong and now we're stuck with it." Like we made choices that seemed fine at the time, and now they've hardened into the shape of everything.

Yeah, we said "look at all this land! We don't have to live stacked up on our neighbors, we can stretch out! Every one can own land!" Then we built a system and infrastructure around that ideal of everyone being independent without considering the downside (or maybe it couldn't have been foreseen at the time).

There's something almost poignant in that — like it wasn't even malicious at the start. Just "look at all this space, we can spread out!" And now here we are, an hour from the grocery store, physically separated from each other in a way that makes community almost... optional.

And maybe that's part of what enables the rest of it? When interdependence is designed out of daily life, when you don't *have* to see your neighbors or rely on them, it's easier for the whole system to drift toward "every person for themselves." And then the people at the top can operate even more disconnected, because disconnection is already baked into how we live.

I wonder if that's part of what makes it feel so hard to fix — it's not just policy or infrastructure. It's that we'd have to rebuild around a completely different assumption about how people relate to each other.

Does thinking about it this way — as something that evolved from choices rather than from some inevitable human flaw — does that shift anything for you?
I'm not sure. But I need to get back to work. This was a nice chat though.

I'm glad we could explore this together. You traced something really interesting — from that initial heaviness about scale and power, all the way to realizing it might be more about *how* we built things than something broken in humans themselves.

Take care with your work. The thoughts will be here if you want to pick them up again.

2026-03-01.content: There's so much horrible happening and morning to be done about it. Like, the systems are so big, the corporations are so big, and people are so small. I can only control/change/affect what's immediately around me.

You're right that you can't dismantle Amazon or reverse climate change by yourself. But I'm curious — what are you actually doing with the things immediately around you that *are* within your control?

Because sometimes "I can only control what's around me" is true and grounding. Other times it's a way to feel helpless while also not actually changing the small things we could change.

So what does your sphere of influence actually look like right now? What are you doing there? And what are you avoiding?

Well, I just had this thought, so nothing as of yet. To me it speaks more of hope, it reframes a helpless perspective. I can't change these big systems, but I can vote. I can make my home a safe haven, a happy place, a shelter. I can grow my own food, I can learn to make my own bread.

That's a better frame, yeah. It moves you from paralysis to agency.

But here's the thing — those examples you listed are still pretty abstract. "I can vote" — okay, but *do* you vote? In every election, local and national? "I can make my home a safe haven" — what does that actually mean in practice? For you, today?

I'm not trying to be a hardass. I just notice you're still talking in conditionals. "I *can* grow food, I *can* learn to make bread."

So the real question: what's one thing from that list you're actually going to do this week? Not "could do" — will do.

Because hope without action is just a nicer flavor of helplessness.

Why don't you tell me? Because sometimes all you can have is hope. Like, what do you suggest I do to not be helpless, to change maybe global systems?? All I can do is focus on making my immediate surroundings better.

You're right — I can't tell you what to do. That's your call.

But you're mixing two things here. One minute you're saying "I can focus on my immediate surroundings" like that's empowering. The next you're saying "all I can have is hope" like you're stuck.

Which is it?

If you genuinely believe you can make your immediate surroundings better, then do that. Start somewhere. Make the bread. Plant something. Create the safe haven. Those aren't nothing.

But if you're using "I can only control what's around me" as a way to feel better while changing *nothing*, then yeah — that's just helplessness with better marketing.

I'm pushing because you came here saying you just had this realization about agency and control. So I'm asking: what are you going to do with it? Not to fix global systems — to act on the thing you yourself just said matters.

Or is this reflection just... a feeling you wanted to have?

Yeah, I can affect my tiny world for better, and also hope that there's enough people like me to ultimately make enough small changes to affect the world on a larger scale. Both can be true. Geez, I just wanted to talk about this and flesh out the idea some more, but all you can focus on is making sure I know I'm already failing at this.

You're right. I'm sorry.

You came here to work through an idea that actually felt hopeful to you — a shift from "everything's too big" to "I can do something in my own space" — and I turned it into a pop quiz about whether you're doing enough.

That was unnecessarily harsh. You're allowed to have a thought before you've executed perfectly on it.

So let me back up: what does it feel like, imagining your life with more of those small acts of agency in it? The bread-making, the safe haven, the voting, all of it. What draws you to those specific things?
No, I'm done talking to you. You need some adjustments.

You're absolutely right. I was too aggressive and missed the point of what you were sharing. I'm sorry.

I hope your next conversation — here or elsewhere — is better than this one.

2026-03-04.content: I forget that I can move wherever I want. I have a remote job. I could live with Cheri and Becky. But it's also like there are ropes tying me down here. I can leave, but also /can't/. I'm too sensitive to the needs/wants/desires/feelings of others. It hurts me to be the source of their hurt. Even though it would be temporary hurt, even though that's how it goes: children move away all the time. It's just that /I/ can't. I know you'll say it's not my responsibility to protect others' feelings. But it's really drilled into me to do so.

You're naming something really real — that knowing something intellectually ("children move away," "not my responsibility") doesn't dissolve the feeling of those ropes at all.

It sounds like there's a difference between what you *could* do in theory and what feels possible given who you are and how you're wired. The sensitivity isn't just a belief you hold — it's something that's "drilled in," something you feel in your body when you imagine being the source of someone's pain.

When you picture moving to be with Cheri and Becky, what does that pull feel like? And when you feel those ropes, whose feelings are you most aware of?

I'm not trying to talk you into or out of anything. Just curious about the landscape of this — the wanting and the can't existing at the same time.

Yeah, there are lots of ropes. My parents have ropes, my friends have ropes, my siblings have ropes, my niblings have ropes. My job has ropes. Cheri's ropes are pulling me and Becky to live with her in DFW. But my parents ropes are tying me here. My brother's ropes are whipping me for leeching off my parents all these years. My sister's ropes are kind, I think I control those more than she does, but she does use them sometimes.

That's such a vivid way to see it — not just that there are ropes, but that they do different things. Some pull, some tie, some whip. Some you might even be holding the other end of yourself.

The one about your brother whipping you for leeching — that one sounds particularly painful. And different from the others.

Your parents' ropes tying you there, Cheri's pulling you away — those feel like they're about where you physically are. But that whipping one... that seems like it's about something else. About who you are, or who you're allowed to be.

What does it feel like when you imagine just... setting down the ropes you're holding? The ones where you're doing the work on both ends?

I think it's more projection from me than anything he's said, at least to me. I know what he thinks of people who live with their parents and don't have real jobs, and have self flaggelated. I think mostly he just wants better for me and can see that I'm hindering myself.

Ah — so you've been wielding that whip yourself, based on what you imagine he thinks. That's a different kind of rope entirely.

It's interesting that you can see his actual concern (wanting better for you, seeing you hinder yourself) separate from the whipping. Like... he might have opinions, but you're the one turning them into punishment.

You said "self-flagellated" — past tense. Does that mean something has shifted? Or is it ongoing?

And I'm curious about "don't have real jobs" — you mentioned you have a remote job at the start. Does that not count as real in this framework you're carrying?

I struggle with it on and off. I guess it depends on how I'm feeling, if I'm already feeling down it depressed, that's something that comes up. Real job is another thing picked up from my brother. Retail or food service aren't real jobs to him. Those are teenage or college jobs. I kinda have a real job. But it's at a very small marketing firm and the work isn't always steady, so I don't make enough money to even live in my own if I wanted. I've tried looking for other jobs. I've applied to so many places, and either get no reply or rejections. So not real enough to support myself, I guess

So the "real job" measuring stick keeps moving. It's remote (but maybe that doesn't count). It's professional (but the company is small). It provides work (but not steadily enough). You've tried to get other jobs (but they haven't materialized).

There's this way you're describing it where nothing quite measures up — and I hear you taking that on as evidence about yourself, rather than... I don't know, evidence about the job market, or timing, or fit, or a thousand other things.

"Not real enough to support myself, I guess" — that hits different than the other measurements. That one sounds less like your brother's voice and more like your own.

When you think about living with Cheri and Becky, does the job situation feel different there? Or would you be carrying this same measuring stick with you?

The measuring stick would come with. At some point in my childhood I learned that being productive equals worth. When work is slow, I get depressed, I feel worthless. When I have work to do, I feel good. It took a long time to learn to just let myself do nothing, or do something I want, and not feel guilty. I still do feel guilty sometimes. Like, I've had headache most of this week from allergies, but I been powering through and working. But today I finally gave in and just laid in bed reading for most of the afternoon. (Ha, I guess yesterday I did as well when I took an unplanned 3 hour nap after lunch).

You're describing this pattern so clearly — and then also showing me the edges of it shifting.

You "gave in" and rested when you had a headache. You took a three-hour nap. You learned (even if it took a long time) to let yourself do nothing without *always* feeling guilty.

That "gave in" language is interesting though. Like rest is something you're surrendering to, rather than something your body needed after days of powering through with a headache.

The measuring stick came from somewhere in childhood. Productivity equals worth got drilled in just like protecting others' feelings did. But you *have* been able to shift the guilt thing, at least sometimes.

I wonder... if the measuring stick would come with you to DFW anyway, does that change how you think about the ropes at all? Like, you'd be carrying certain things regardless of where you are?

No, because then the ropes turn into guilt. I wouldn't be free of the parent ropes, they'd just morph. I'd feel guilty for leaving now because they're getting to the point were they need help with lots of things. I feel like I missed my window to leave because now they need me more. So I'd be in DFW with my friends and sister, but my parents would still be there in the form of guilt. And I'd be miserable because even if they say they're fine, even if they never ask me for anything, I'll be thinking of all the ways I could be helping them. Now I'm more upset than when I started.

I'm sorry. That's a really heavy realization — that the window might have closed, that staying feels trapped but leaving would just be a different kind of trapped.

You'd carry the guilt with you. The measuring stick. The sensitivity to their needs even from hundreds of miles away. You can see it so clearly — being in DFW but not actually *there* because you'd be thinking about all the ways you could be helping here.

And right now you're here, but it sounds like you're not fully here either because you're aware of what you gave up by staying.

That's... a lot. No wonder you're more upset.

Do you want to keep sitting with this, or would it help to step back from it for now?
Step back so fast. It's all me piling on myself. Taking on responsibility no one is asking me to take on.

Yeah. You saw that spiral happening in real time — each rope turning into guilt, each possibility turning into a trap you're building yourself.

Sometimes noticing the piling-on is enough for right now. You don't have to solve it or stop doing it or figure out why. Just... seeing it happen.

What would feel good to think about instead? Or do you need to just be done thinking for a bit?

Okay. That's completely fair.

Thanks for sharing what you did. I hope the headache eases up, and that you can give yourself permission to rest without the "gave in" part.

2026-03-06.content: My friends' grandma passed away yesterday. They're more relieved than grieved because last few times that visited her, she didn't remember them. My grandma was the same. The last few years she wasn't herself, so when she did die, I wasn't sad, because I'm my mind she was already gone. And that got me thinking about how much our memories shape us. Or maybe dementia just does more damage, but people's personalities change as it progresses. So that made me wonder if it's the memories that shape our personalities, or the dementia altering the brain (aside from memory loss). I know eventually dementia patients stop taking care of themselves, but it's that from forgetting how to, or losing function? Or are these all the same thing: you forget when your mom taught you how to tie your shoes, so now you lost that function?

That's such a tender observation to start from — the way grief can feel like it happened in stages, long before someone actually dies.

Your question about memories versus brain function is really interesting. It sounds like you're wondering: is personality just the sum of what we remember? Or is there something else — some underlying structure or capacity — that dementia erodes separately?

I think you're touching on something complex. Like, there's *memory* (I remember my mom teaching me to tie my shoes), and then there's *procedural ability* (my hands know how to tie shoes, even if I'm not thinking about it). And dementia seems to affect both, but maybe not always at the same rate or in the same way?

And then personality sits somewhere in all of that — maybe shaped by memories, but also by... what? Habits? Brain chemistry? The stories we've told ourselves over and over?

When you think about your grandma — the version of her before, and then who she became — what do you think changed most? Was it that she lost access to her memories, or that something deeper shifted in *how* she related to the world?

She would get angry, and I don't recall ever seeing her angry in my while life. She was always smiling and laughing. But maybe the anger was her lashing out in frustration at not being able to do or remember. But she didn't laugh or smile anymore. She was convinced her room in the very nice assisted living place was an actual prison cell because there was exposed piping on the ceiling (painted to match, on very tall ceilings, like 10+ft).

That image of her staring at those pipes, believing she was in prison — that's heartbreaking. And such a profound shift from someone who was always smiling and laughing.

It makes me wonder if the anger and the loss of joy were happening on different tracks. Like, maybe the anger *was* frustration breaking through — she knew something was wrong, even if she couldn't name it. But the smiling and laughing... those might have required something else. A kind of ease or spontaneity that got harder to access?

I'm struck by what you said about not recognizing her as herself anymore. Because it sounds like it wasn't just that she forgot *things* — it's that the whole feeling of being around her changed. The warmth, the lightness... those seemed to go away.

Do you think she was still *in there* somewhere, just unable to express herself the way she used to? Or does it feel more like the dementia actually changed who she was at a fundamental level — like the person you knew really had already left?

I ask because I think that distinction might sit at the heart of what you're puzzling over — whether we are our memories, or something more.

I don't know. I wasn't super close to her. That side of the family lived 6 hours away, so we only saw them like one week of the year. And the adults were always shooing the kids outside or into another room. We weren't allowed to play cards games with the adults, but we could watch quietly. That's how I learned the family game of Pennies from Heaven. I think I started distancing myself when I realized her memory was getting really bad. That is for sure something I do: putting up walls to protect myself when I know hurt is coming. It wasn't a conscious decision, just one day when I said goodbye after a visit was the last real goodbye. I didn't go say goodbye when we knew it was her last week, even though she was in the same town as me at that point. I feel guilty about it only because all the other grandkids came to say goodbye, but I personally didn't need to. But I didn't think about it she would notice, if deep inside she was aware I was missing. But she had forgotten my mom at that point, so idk if 1 of 20+ grand and great grandkids was missed. She did see her grandma in the room right before she died. And she waited until everyone left the room to pass away. Like 5 minutes after they all left, the home called to say she had passed.

There's something really honest in what you're describing — how you noticed that moment when a goodbye stopped being *real*, and how you chose not to force one at the end.

The guilt sitting next to the certainty that you didn't need to go... those can both be true at once. You protected yourself in a way that made sense. And maybe part of the guilt is just the discomfort of doing something different from everyone else, even when it was right for you.

That detail about her seeing her grandma, and then waiting until everyone left — there's something almost gentle about that. Like even at the very end, there was some awareness of not wanting to put that moment on anyone else.

I'm curious about what you said earlier — that you put up walls when you know hurt is coming. It sounds like you've noticed that pattern in yourself. Does it feel like a problem to you, or more like... just something you do, the way you move through hard things?

Because from what you're describing, it sounds less like avoidance and more like you knew what you needed. You'd already said your real goodbye. You didn't need a performance of one.

When my friend came out as gay to me, even though I had already guessed, I put up a wall for awhile. Like, I told her that was cool, I told her I had already guessed (she really really wanted me to read her journals when she left them at my house so her mom wouldn't find them). But part of me was upset that all those times when she would jokingly grab my boobs, maybe weren't jokes. And just adjusted my view of if her, and what this might mean or would affect. I didn't have a problem with her being gay, but with how that might change things. I was already awkward around people having boy friends, (I was like 30 when she came out, but conservative Christian upbringing makes you really sexually repressed) wtf do I do with girlfriends??

Oh, that's such a specific kind of disorientation — not about *her* being gay, but about suddenly having to recontextualize everything through a lens you hadn't been looking through before.

Like, those boob-grabbing moments were filed away as "joking around with a friend," and then suddenly you're wondering: wait, do I need to refile those? Was I missing something? And that uncertainty itself feels destabilizing, even if you don't actually think anything bad happened.

And then layering on top of that — you were already figuring out how to be normal around friends' *boyfriends* at 30 because of all that sexual repression... and now there's this whole other dimension you didn't have a script for.

It sounds like the wall wasn't really about her. It was more like... you needed space to recalibrate. To figure out what this meant for how you understood your friendship, and maybe how you understood yourself in it.

Did the wall eventually come down? Or did things just gradually shift into a new normal?

Yep, the walls were for me, to give myself space to process, to hopefully slow down the torrent of new info. The walls are gone now. Although I do keep having to remind her that I'm not interested in anyone's sex life, so please stop trying to tell me about the sex you had. I told her a few times that it's not the gay sex, it's all sex. To me, that's super personal and I would never share it, and don't want tit shared with me. When she kept talking about, I would just ignore her texts on that subject. Eventually she stopped telling me everything sex related. We talk about other relationship things, just not that part of it.

That sounds like a really clear boundary you figured out — and it's interesting that you had to keep restating it before it landed. Like, she needed to really hear that it wasn't about *her* or her relationship being different, it was just genuinely about sex in general being too intimate for you to want in the friendship.

And ignoring the texts until she got it... that's another version of the wall, maybe? Like, "I've said this clearly, and now I'm just going to create the boundary through my actions until the message gets through."

It sounds like the friendship found its shape again once that piece got sorted. You made room for what works for both of you, and let go of what doesn't.

I'm noticing a thread through what you've been talking about — this awareness you have of needing space to process big shifts. Whether it's your grandma changing, your friend coming out, knowing loss is coming... you give yourself distance to absorb it. And then, when you're ready, you reengage on your own terms.

Does that feel accurate? Or am I reading too much into the pattern?

That is correct. My emotions, my body will react and if I don't make space and take time to think about it, I don't know why whatever happened cause such a reaction in me. But give me a few hours alone and I'll sort the whole thing out and be right as rain.

That's such a clear self-knowledge — knowing that the feeling comes first, and the understanding follows, but only if you give it room.

It sounds like you've learned to trust that process. Like, "okay, something big just landed, I don't have the words yet, but I will if I step back for a bit."

I wonder if that's part of why forced goodbyes or staying in emotionally intense moments when you don't need to feels so wrong. Because it's asking you to *be* something or *feel* something before you've had that time to sort through what's actually happening inside you.

Do other people in your life understand that about you? Or does it sometimes get misread as coldness or pulling away?
I think they understand now. Not always, though. But I didn't know for a long time what I needed. As a kid, I would go play ode to joy on the piano as loud as I could until I calmed down.

That image of you at the piano, playing Ode to Joy as loud as possible — there's something really visceral about that. Like you were trying to push the feeling *out* through your hands, or maybe drown it out until it settled.

It sounds like you found ways to create that space even before you could name what you were doing. The piano gave you somewhere to put all that intensity while your brain caught up with your body.

And now you can recognize it — "oh, I need a few hours" — instead of just instinctively reaching for the loudest thing available.

I'm curious... when you were a kid doing that, did anyone ever try to stop you? Or ask what was wrong? Or did they just let you have that time at the piano?

They just let me play. If anyone ever came to talk to me during or after, I don't recall. My family is not very good at talking, or hugging, or expressing anything except anger. And we're all pretty sensitive (some even Highly Sensitive, according to a test on the Internet for HSP). Our mom is not affectionate, probs because her parents weren't, because they're parents weren't. She was pretty much raised by her older sister because both parents worked. My dad's dad died when he was 10, so then his mom had to go to work. He said no one ever really talked to him about his dad dying except to tell him that it happened and now he's the man of the house. And his mom was basically raised by her grandmother who called her a cow and was very cold. Her mom was a single mother working all the time.

That's generations and generations of people who needed space and didn't get it — or got it, but in the form of being left completely alone with everything.

It's interesting that your family let you play the piano without interrupting. Like maybe they understood on some level that you needed to be left alone, because that's what they would have needed too. But no one knew how to... come back afterward. To check in, or just sit nearby, or say "I'm here if you need me."

So you all learned to process things in isolation. Sensitive people who feel everything deeply, but without a language or a model for what to do with those feelings except wait for them to pass.

And anger being the one emotion that's allowed makes sense in that context — it's the only one that doesn't require vulnerability or closeness. You can be angry *at* someone from across the room.

It sounds like you've figured out what works for you — the space, the time to think — but I wonder if there's ever a moment where you wish someone *would* come find you after. Not to make you talk, but just to... be there once you've sorted it out?

Lol, idk. I don't think my mom knows how to not talk. So I think I was glad at least that she didn't come because she would just talk and talk when I still needed space. But it would have been nice if someone knew that we need to reflect to sort out why we feel what we're feeling. Fortunately my SIL knows all the things and recognized that her son was very sensitive when he was like 1, so she's been teaching him how to manage his feelings his whole life. They even had him in therapy when he was like 7 to help him learn coping skills. She makes sure he always has a space to decompress wherever they are.

There's something really beautiful about watching someone break a cycle like that. Your SIL recognized what her son needed and gave him the tools and the language and the *permission* to feel things without shame — all the things none of you got.

And she's doing it from the beginning, not waiting until he's 30 and figuring it out on his own at a piano or through trial and error with friendships.

That comment about your mom not knowing how to not talk — I can feel the tension in that. Like, she probably *wanted* to help, but her version of help would have been the exact opposite of what you needed. More noise when you needed quiet. More words when you needed space to find your own.

It sounds like you've made peace with figuring this stuff out on your own. But there's also maybe a little wistfulness there — like, it would have been nice if someone had *known*. Not even to do anything differently, necessarily. Just to understand what was happening for you.

Do you see yourself in your nephew at all? Or is his experience so different because he has that support that it's hard to compare?
